Health Ministry warns public of risk of heat-related illnesses
The Ministry of Health and Child Care has urged Zimbabweans to take precautions against extreme heat, warning that prolonged exposure to high temperatures could lead to serious illness and even death.
In a public advisory issued on Thursday, 5 November, the ministry said the country is experiencing a hot period during which high temperatures, direct sunlight and strenuous physical activity can overwhelm the body’s natural cooling system.
The ministry warned that this could result in dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, a potentially fatal medical emergency.
The warning comes as Zimbabwe prepares for a season that is expected to bring below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures.
“The 2026/2027 seasonal climate outlook indicates the likelihood of below-normal rainfall and warmer-than-normal temperatures associated with El Niño conditions, potentially increasing heat exposure and water stress,” the ministry said.
Health officials said although anyone can be affected by extreme heat, certain groups face a greater risk. These include children, elderly people, pregnant women, people living with chronic illnesses, persons with disabilities and those who work outdoors, such as farmers, construction workers and street vendors.
To reduce the risk of heat-related illnesses, the ministry advised members of the public to drink safe water regularly, even when they do not feel thirsty. People have also been encouraged to avoid unnecessary outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, particularly from late morning to mid-afternoon.
The ministry further urged Zimbabweans to seek shade, remain in cool and well-ventilated places and wear light, loose-fitting clothing. It also called on families to check regularly on vulnerable relatives and warned against leaving children unattended in parked vehicles.
Employers have been urged to protect outdoor workers by providing clean drinking water, shaded rest areas and regular breaks.
The ministry also stressed the importance of recognising the early signs of heat exhaustion, which include heavy sweating, severe thirst, headaches, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
People displaying such symptoms should be moved to a cool place, have excess clothing loosened and be given water if they are fully alert and able to drink.
However, health authorities stressed that heatstroke is a medical emergency requiring immediate attention.
According to the ministry, warning signs of heatstroke include confusion, unusual behaviour, seizures, collapse or loss of consciousness following exposure to extreme heat. The affected person’s skin may be hot and dry or heavily sweaty.
“Do not wait for all symptoms to appear,” the ministry warned.
The ministry said anyone suspected of suffering from heatstroke should be taken to a cool place and cooled immediately using cold water, wet cloths and fanning while emergency medical assistance is sought.
“Continue cooling while awaiting medical assistance,” the ministry said.
Health officials also warned against giving fluids to anyone unconscious, confused or unable to swallow properly, and warned that medicines such as paracetamol and aspirin should not be used to treat heatstroke.

▲ Snowy and rainy weather
Moving beyond "ultra-strong," the "strongest" El Niño is expected to continue this winter.
The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) stated that the El Niño that began in May is anticipated to become the "strongest El Niño on record."
El Niño is officially recognized as having begun when the 3-month moving average of sea surface temperatures in the El Niño-La Niña monitoring region of the tropical Pacific remains 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) higher than normal for five months or more.
According to the KMA, the sea surface temperature in the El Niño-La Niña monitoring region from October 11 to 17 was 30.0 degrees Celsius (86.0 degrees Fahrenheit), which was 3.3 degrees Celsius (5.9 degrees Fahrenheit) higher than normal.
A deviation of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) or more from normal is classified as a "strong El Niño," meaning this baseline has been significantly surpassed.
The deviation from normal sea surface temperatures in the El Niño-La Niña monitoring region was 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) for October and 2.4 degrees Celsius (4.3 degrees Fahrenheit) based on the August–October moving average.
The KMA explained that this is the largest deviation since records began in 1950, surpassing the records set during the strong El Niño events of 1997 and 2015.
El Niño occurs when the trade winds (easterlies), which normally push warm surface water in the tropical Pacific toward the western Pacific, weaken. As a result, the warm surface water accumulated in the western Pacific spreads to the central and eastern Pacific, raising sea surface temperatures in these regions and creating an energy circulation pattern different from usual.
El Niño is not a consequence of climate change and is a "natural" phenomenon, with official records dating back to 1881.
However, it affects global weather and also fuels global warming.
El Niño typically strengthens in the winter, and the current El Niño is projected to peak in December.
The KMA forecasted, "Sea surface temperatures in the El Niño-La Niña monitoring region are expected to remain high, developing into the strongest El Niño on record."
When El Niño occurs, convective activity in the tropical western Pacific weakens, and anticyclonic circulation frequently develops in the Philippine Sea and to the east of South Korea.
Consequently, warm and humid southerly winds ride along the edge of this anticyclonic circulation into the country, resulting in higher temperatures and increased precipitation.
At the Korean Meteorological Society conference last month, a research team led by Professor Kuk Jong-seong of Seoul National University stated that during strong El Niño development years—1982/83, 1997/98, and 2015/16—precipitation in November, the El Niño development period, was more than double that of an average November.
In its 3-month outlook released on October 23, the KMA predicted that temperatures in November and December would be higher and precipitation greater than normal, while for January of next year, temperatures would be higher than normal and precipitation similar to normal.
However, the KMA emphasized, "Winter weather is influenced by various climatic factors in addition to El Niño, such as sea surface temperatures in the Indian and Atlantic Oceans, Arctic sea ice, and Eurasian snow cover, so the latest forecasts should be checked."

Christchurch City Council is warning of an increased risk of unpleasant smells from its wastewater treatment plant after conditions in two oxidation ponds deteriorated this week.
Ponds 1 and 2A have moved to red on the council’s odour status tracker, indicating a high probability of smells affecting nearby areas. Pond 2B has moved to orange as similar signs of declining health begin to emerge.
However, the council said its community monitoring network had not recorded any significant spikes in recent days.
The decline comes while Clarifier 4 is offline for essential repairs, directing more load to the oxidation ponds and placing additional pressure on the system.
The council said staff were adjusting loading and flows across the ponds to support their health. Of the plant’s 41 aerators, 39 were operating, with two temporarily offline because of an electrical issue.
“We know the potential for odour is a concern for residents, particularly those living near the treatment plant,” the council said.
“Please be assured we are closely tracking conditions and will provide a further update early next week.”
Repair work on Clarifier 4 remained on track, with the unit expected to return to service in early December.
Clarifiers use gravity to separate solids and suspended particles from wastewater before it flows to the oxidation ponds for final treatment.
The work includes a full overhaul of the drive mechanism powering Clarifier 4’s rotating arms. The council said replacing the system would improve reliability and reduce the risk of further problems as the equipment reached the end of its service life.
The overhaul would also help prepare the clarifier to support the new activated sludge plant when it comes online.
In an earlier update, the council said pond conditions remained significantly better than during the major odour problems earlier this year. However, it warned there could be patches of odour in the coming days and weeks while Clarifier 4 remained out of service.
The council said odour could be worse overnight and early in the morning, when still air allowed gas to accumulate and drift slowly into nearby areas. Oxygen levels in the ponds also dropped overnight because algae stopped producing oxygen in the absence of sunlight.
Residents who notice odour are encouraged to report its location and strength through the council’s Smelt-it reporting tool.
Hourly average hydrogen sulphide readings from community monitors are also available on the council’s monitoring dashboard.
